# topic: Sir Gawain Part 2 (Fitt III)
# short: 4 Main Ideas
# order: 4
# expect: 22
How the first morning hunt begins
column2: As morning lifts its lamp, Bertilak and his huntsmen ride high on horseback, and bugles blow three long bare notes while hounds bay through the trees.

column1: Why only female deer are killed
column2: Bertilak has laid down a law that man should not maim the male in close season, so stags and bucks pass while hinds and does are driven and shot.

column1: How Lady Bertilak enters on day 1
column2: While Gawain slumbers, Lady Bertilak slyly opens the door, creeps inside the curtains, sits at his bedside, and waits until he stirs from false sleep.

column1: Lady Bertilak's day-1 invitation
column2: Alone with the door barred, Lady Bertilak tells Gawain he is free to have her all, do with her what he will, and she will come just as he calls.

column1: How Gawain handles the first temptation
column2: Gawain acts graciously and remains on guard, countering every move case by case, cool in his conduct because he foresees the strike he must receive.

column1: Why Lady Bertilak rebukes Gawain's name
column2: Lady Bertilak says a good man like Gawain, the embodiment of courtliness to the bones of his being, could never linger so long without craving a kiss as politeness requires.

column1: The first evening exchange
column2: Bertilak gives Gawain the whole deer haul as the contract claims, and Gawain returns one kiss but refuses to confess by what wit he won it, saying that wasn't our pact, so don't pry.

column1: How the second day's boar hunt ends
column2: The boar stands at bay until Bertilak wades through water, knives the boar's neck, nails his prey, and bursts the hog's heart, then the head is borne before the lord.

column1: Lady Bertilak's day-2 love lesson
column2: Lady Bertilak asks how the most notable knight can sit twice at her side without speaking the smallest syllable which belongs to love, urging him to lead her as pupil in love's art.

column1: How Gawain answers the love challenge
column2: Gawain praises her insight, declines to explain true love to someone more skilled than he, yet vows to the best of his ability to do her bidding as her servant.

column1: The second evening exchange
column2: Bertilak gives Gawain the boar as the wager warranted, and Gawain returns two kisses, so Bertilak says he has tested Gawain twice and found him truthful.

column1: Why Bertilak keeps Gawain for a third day
column2: Gawain pleads to leave so he can honor his Green Chapel treaty, but Bertilak swears the chapel is near and tells him to think tomorrow third time throw best.

column1: How the third-day fox hunt runs
column2: Hounds fall on a fox's scent and chase crafty Reynard through mountains until midafternoon, when Bertilak heaves the fox up and the red fur is prised from its pelt.

column1: Lady Bertilak's third-day pressure
column2: Lady Bertilak says Gawain shall bear the blame if he feels no love for the lady he lies with, unless another lady already holds a bond that will not break.

column1: Gawain's claim of no other lady
column2: Gawain smiles and swears by Saint John there is no other one, nor will be for this while, which Lady Bertilak calls the worst of all answers.

column1: How the green girdle is offered
column2: After Gawain refuses a rich red-gold ring, Lady Bertilak unbuckles her green silk girdle trimmed with gold and begs him to receive it in spite of its slightness.

column1: What power Lady Bertilak claims for the girdle
column2: Lady Bertilak says the body bound within this green belt, as long as it is buckled robustly about him, will be safe against anyone who seeks to strike him, and all the slyness on earth wouldn't see him slain.

column1: Why Gawain finally takes the girdle
column2: Gawain mulls that it might be the jewel for the jeopardy he faces and save him from the strike at the chapel, so with luck it might let him escape with his life.

column1: The secrecy condition on the girdle
column2: Lady Bertilak begs Gawain not to whisper a word of this gift to her husband, and Gawain agrees that those words within those walls should stay.

column1: How Gawain hides the love-lace
column2: After the third kiss he stows the love-lace safely aside, hiding it away from all hands and eyes, then goes to confess to the priest.

column1: The third evening's incomplete exchange
column2: Gawain returns three kisses as presents perfect and true, while Bertilak offers only a foul-stinking fox and never receives the girdle Gawain gained.

column1: How the hunt-temptation structure tests trouthe
column2: Each day's more cunning quarry (deer, boar, fox) mirrors a sharper bedroom test, until the fox-day secrecy breaks the exchange-of-winnings bargain even as courtesy and chastity largely hold.
